questions.prompt: Which mechanisms enforce the Dependency Rule mechanically (so it can't erode)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Module visibility that hides a component's internals so illegal imports won't compile
A dependency linter that fails the CI build on forbidden imports
Architecture tests (e.g., ArchUnit) asserting allowed dependencies

questions.explanation: Module visibility, dependency linters, and architecture tests make the rule a build gate. Relying on memory or discipline alone is exactly what lets boundaries erode.

options.text: A single deployable unit with strong, enforced internal module boundaries

questions.explanation: A modular monolith gives much of the changeability of separate services through enforced internal boundaries, without the network and deployment costs.

questions.prompt: The same architectural boundary can be implemented at different strengths and later ______ (e.g., source → module → service) as pressure justifies.
questions.explanation: Boundary strength is a spectrum; start with the cheapest effective form and upgrade only when a real force appears.

questions.prompt: Order the boundary forms from weakest/cheapest to strongest/costliest.

items.text: Source-level discipline (an interface, a folder rule)

questions.explanation: From cheapest/weakest to strongest/costliest: a source convention, a compile-enforced module, a deployment component, then a separate service.

questions.prompt: Match each packaging strategy to what it groups by.

pairs.right: Encapsulated components with one public entry point

questions.explanation: Most Clean Architecture codebases land on by-feature or by-component at the top, layering within a feature.

questions.prompt: A startup splits a small app into eight microservices 'for clean boundaries,' with no scaling or team-autonomy need. What's the likely result?

options.text: Premature cost: lost local reasoning, coordinated deploys, and distributed debugging that a modular monolith would have avoided

questions.explanation: They jumped to the strongest, most expensive boundary form without a real force; a modular monolith would have given the same isolation far more cheaply.
